This page covers the parts of the toolchain specific to the **Reproducible
Workflows** course: Quarto, Python (via `uv`), git, and publishing. It assumes
you already have R, Positron and the core R packages from the companion
[Setup · common](setup-common.qmd) page.

## 1. Install Quarto

Quarto is our open-source scientific and technical publishing system. It turns
`.qmd` documents (and RevealJS slides!) into polished HTML, PDF, and more.

- Download: <https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/>

Check it works:

```bash
quarto --version   # e.g. 1.10.x
```

## 2. Version control with git

Everything in this course is versioned with **git**. Install it first, then set
your identity.

```bash
git --version                    # e.g. 2.4x.x
```

For Windows users, follow <https://happygitwithr.com/install-git>. On
macOS/Linux, git usually ships with the OS or the Xcode command-line tools.

Your `git` identity should match the account you use on **GitHub**, where your
repositories will be hosted. If you do not have one yet, create a free account
at <https://github.com>. Then set the same name and email you used there as your
global `git` identity:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

If you are already working in R, [`usethis::use_git_config()`](https://usethis.r-lib.org) walks
you through setting these same values; [`usethis`](https://usethis.r-lib.org) and `gitcreds`
are handy companions for all the Session 2/3 git work (see <https://happygitwithr.com/hello-git>).

The required R packages for the git work are `usethis` and `gitcreds`, both
installed in [Setup · common](setup-common.qmd). **Reference guide:** <https://happygitwithr.com/>.

### Personal access tokens (PAT)

You need to grant Positron permissions to act on the behalf of your GitHub
account. The recommended way nowadays is to create a personal access token (PAT)
on GitHub and register it in Positron.

While you can create it directly from the GitHub interface online and then
register it manually, `usethis` makes it one command:

```r
usethis::create_github_token()
```

This command requests to open a web browser page for PAT creation with
appropriate options already checked.

- Proceed with creating the PAT.
- Copy the PAT to clipboard with the button.

Then, back in Positron, do:

```r
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
```

Follow the instructions, paste the PAT and validate. `git push` and
`usethis::use_github()` then authenticate automatically.

### Structure your work and push to GitHub

Take the habit of creating a dedicated folder for each project and opening it in
Positron as working directory, then initialize version control on it:

```r
usethis::use_git()
```

In Positron you can access the Git pane in the left sidebar. Once your project
is committed locally, push a remote copy to GitHub:

```r
usethis::use_github()
```

## 3. Publishing with Posit Connect

Session 3 reports are published to **Posit Connect**, the server that puts your
work live at a URL. There is nothing to install, but you do need an **account**
on the server: a free-tier account is sufficient for this course. The instructor
will hand out the sign-up URL in Session 3. Then you publish from inside Quarto
with `quarto publish connect`.

## 4. Pinning a whole project with `uvr`

For the Reproducible Workflows course you pin a **whole project**, not just one
machine: the R version *and* every package's version, so the project re-runs
identically next year on another machine. That is what `uvr` does. It is a thin
wrapper that lets R use `uv` (the same Rust project manager that drives the
Python setup below). Install it from GitHub, then install its binary:

```r
pak::pak("nbafrank/uvr-r")   # the uvr companion R package
uvr::install_uvr()           # installs the uvr binary (cross-platform)
```

Inside a project folder (`uvr::init()`), `uvr` manages a **project-local** R
(`uvr::r_install("4.6.1")`, `uvr::r_pin("4.6.1")`) and adds packages to a
manifest + lockfile with `uvr::add("tidyverse")`. So `uvr` is not only about
which R version you run: it installs **and** pins every dependency behind a
lockfile. That makes it the project-scoped alternative to the r2u /
`install.packages()` / `pak::pak()` routes in [Setup · common](setup-common.qmd).
Use those to get R and packages working machine-wide; reach for `uvr` once you
are inside a real project you need to reproduce.

## 5. Setup Python (optional)

In Positron:

- Open the palette with the keyboard shortcut `CMD + SHIFT + P`;
- Search for `Python: install Python via uv` and proceed.

More at <https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-07-08_positron-uv/>

## 6. Install Python packages (optional)

[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) is an extremely fast Python package and project
manager, written in Rust.

You can easily install Python packages in dedicated virtual environments with
`uv`. For example, to install the `pandas` and `numpy` packages, run in the
Positron-integrated terminal:

```bash
uv init example
# Initialized project `example` at `/home/user/example`
uv add pandas numpy
```

More details can be found on the website.
